tldr: By integrating spiral springs and clutches into an inexpensive 3D-printed leader arm to provide a physical restoring force pulling joints toward a neutral posture, this work drastically reduces posture variance in imitation learning data and dramatically boosts task success rates.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed Hardware-as-Regularization approach. Using a passive joint module built solely from 3D-printed parts, a spring, and an encoder, the operator's posture naturally settles toward a neutral posture during teleoperation. This mechanically solves an $L_2$ regularization problem, enhancing data consistency.
overview:
To scale imitation learning for robotics (learning behaviors by mimicking human demonstrations), low-cost 3D-printed teleoperation devices (leader arms) such as GELLO and ALOHA are rapidly spreading. However, conventional budget arms are completely limp structures that merely measure joint angles. When a robot arm has redundant joints—more degrees of freedom than strictly required to position the end-effector—arm postures such as elbow height vary wildly across teleoperation trials even when reaching the exact same end-effector location. This posture inconsistency (null-space drift) is a major culprit behind degraded policy performance.

To address this, the authors came up with the idea of "Hardware-as-Regularization"—making the hardware itself act as an optimization regularization term. Instead of relying on active motor control, which is expensive and carries risks of latency and oscillation, they integrated an inexpensive 3D-printed spiral spring and an adjustable clutch mechanism into each joint. Leveraging the human tendency to subconsciously minimize muscular effort, the restoring force pulling joints back to a neutral position becomes mathematically equivalent to joint-space $L_2$ regularization (Tikhonov regularization).

In experiments, the authors conducted stiffness evaluations using a torque wrench, simulation studies on posture consistency and smoothness, and real-robot (OpenArm) imitation learning tasks like block stacking. The results showed a drastic drop in joint-angle variance compared to a conventional limp arm, doubling the success rate on the block stacking task from 36.7% to 73.3%. This demonstrates that a completely passive mechanism can match or exceed the smoothness and consistency of an active virtual spring driven by motors, all without extra computational overhead or electrical latency.
contributions: Developed a low-cost, fully passive joint module equipped with a 3D-printed polycarbonate spiral spring and a Hirth coupling-based clutch
Formulated the concept of "Hardware-as-Regularization", showing that physical hardware stiffness serves as joint-space $L_2$ regularization (structural prior) in redundant teleoperation

Demonstrated that physical spring constraints suppress posture variance in demonstration data and eliminate the backlash catch found in motorized virtual springs, yielding exceptionally smooth trajectories

Showed in downstream imitation learning (ACT) that task success rates improve substantially over conventional passive arms, and that mechanical stiffness directly dictates consistency as a regularization weight

sections.heading: Why does data from budget teleoperation arms drift so much?
sections.summary: Low-cost passive leader arms used in modern imitation learning lack restoring forces, causing redundant joint postures to drift heavily across trials. This study proposes "Hardware-as-Regularization", a new paradigm applying joint-space $L_2$ regularization directly through fully passive mechanical spring modules.
sections.details:
Collecting massive amounts of demonstration data is essential for scaling imitation learning in robotic manipulation. Consequently, low-cost leader arms that can be fabricated using 3D printers, such as GELLO and ALOHA, have gained worldwide adoption.

Yet, they suffer from an overlooked mechanical drawback. In eliminating motorized restoring forces to cut costs, their redundant degrees of freedom—joints beyond what is strictly necessary to determine end-effector pose—are left unconstrained. Due to gravity and the operator's arm position, joint angles such as elbow height drift significantly across trials even during the exact same task. This introduces multi-modal data where identical situations yield conflicting joint commands, greatly hurting the learning efficiency of behavioral cloning.

Classical robotics resolves redundancy via active impedance control (software-generated spring-damper behavior) using expensive motors. However, this contradicts the goal of democratizing low-cost data collection. Furthermore, emulating virtual springs with inexpensive motors easily induces high-frequency oscillations due to communication and control delays, while heavy damping makes the teleoperation feel excessively sluggish.

To circumvent this, the authors turned to the concept of passive haptics. By embedding fully mechanical springs directly into the joints—introducing zero electrical delay and injecting no active energy—the operator's posture can naturally be guided back to a reference position. This is the core concept behind "Hardware-as-Regularization".

captions.F1: Conceptual diagram of Hardware-as-Regularization. A joint module built solely from low-cost mechanical parts physically solves an optimization problem that satisfies workspace constraints while minimizing deviation from a neutral posture $q_0$.

sections.heading: Imitation learning bottlenecks and passive hardware approaches
sections.summary: Even cutting-edge generative models like Diffusion Policy encounter performance ceilings due to kinematic inconsistencies in the data. This study embeds physical compliance into the hardware itself rather than relying on active control that strains control-loop stability limits.
sections.details:
To situate this work, let us review the related literature:

- Low-cost teleoperation and imitation learning: ALOHA and GELLO democratized data collection, but their unconstrained null-space motion creates large variance, leading to distribution shifts that complicate behavioral cloning.
- Generative policies and variance bottlenecks: While recent models such as Diffusion Policy and FlowPolicy boast high expressive capacity, unconstrained joint noise wastes network capacity on fitting arbitrary variations. This is especially problematic in joint space, which directly impacts execution stability.
- Passivity and virtual fixtures in redundant control: Creating virtual stiffness within discrete-time control loops easily violates passivity limits (energy mismatch), triggering unstable oscillations. Passive haptics research using mechanical brakes or springs avoids this, and the proposed method builds on this lineage.
- Operator effort in teleoperation: Human motor control models (such as the minimum-jerk model) indicate that humans subconsciously minimize effort and maximize smoothness. When hardware exerts an elastic restoring force, operators naturally settle into the posture that minimizes physical exertion, providing the theoretical foundation for this approach.

sections.heading: How springs solve L2 regularization, and the adjustable joint design
sections.summary: Minimizing spring potential energy is mathematically identical to Tikhonov regularization ($L_2$ regularization). Mechanically, the authors designed bidirectional 3D-printed spiral springs and Hirth coupling clutches that allow adjusting the neutral posture in 20-degree increments.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Formulating the Consistency Problem in Redundant Arms
The relationship between end-effector displacement $\Delta x$ and joint displacement $\Delta q$ is expressed via the Jacobian $J$ as $\Delta x = J \Delta q$. The inverse kinematics solution is given by $\Delta q = J^+ \Delta x + (I - J^+ J) z$, where $(I - J^+ J) z$ denotes null-space motion that does not affect end-effector position.

In an unconstrained arm, this arbitrary vector $z$ is left uncontrolled, allowing postures to drift due to gravity or hand tremors. Introducing a mechanical spring with neutral posture $q_0$ and stiffness matrix $K$ introduces a potential energy $U(q) = \frac{1}{2}(q-q_0)^T K (q-q_0)$. As human operators subconsciously minimize physical effort, they naturally solve an optimization problem that minimizes $U(q)$ subject to satisfying the target end-effector pose $f(q) = x_d$. When $K$ is positive-definite, the objective function is strictly convex, converging to a unique optimal posture $q^*$. In machine learning terms, this is identical to Tikhonov regularization ($L_2$ regularization).

### 3.2 Mechanical Design Details
The hardware faced two design requirements: a modular structure adaptable across joints, and the ability to easily reconfigure the neutral posture $q_0$ for different tasks.

- Clutch mechanism: Links are connected via a Hirth coupling (featuring radial interlocking teeth) secured by a set screw. Loosening the screw allows free rotation over a bearing, letting the user reset the neutral position in 20-degree increments.
- Bidirectional spiral spring: While conventional torsion coil springs only work in one direction, a planar spiral geometry provides smooth restoring forces in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions from the neutral posture.
- Materials and 3D printing choices: FDM 3D printing is inherently weak against Z-axis tensile stresses. However, a spiral geometry routes filaments continuously in the XY plane, making it exceptionally resilient against bending stresses. Polycarbonate (PC) was chosen for its fatigue and plastic-deformation resistance, while lightweight ABS was used for the outer housings.

captions.F2: Exploded view of the proposed passive joint module. A PC spiral spring, a Hirth coupling for discrete neutral posture adjustments, and a coaxial magnetic encoder are packaged compactly together.

sections.heading: From stiffness testing to real-robot imitation learning: empirical results
sections.summary: The authors evaluated stiffness with a torque wrench, reaching motions in simulation, and imitation learning on a real arm. The passive module sidesteps the backlash deadband of motorized virtual springs and outperforms naive passive arms in real-world tasks (73.3% vs. 36.7% success rate).
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Five participants (1 expert and 4 teleoperation novices) performed tasks using a 7-DoF arm. The benchmark compared three setups: (1) conventional unregularized GELLO (Naive), (2) motorized virtual spring GELLO (Virtual Spring), and (3) GELLO equipped with the proposed module.

### 4.2 Stiffness Analysis: Physical Spring vs. Virtual Spring
Torque-displacement profiles were recorded using a digital torque wrench. The proposed module exhibited clean linearity at $0.0330\text{ Nm/rad}$, showing zero mechanical degradation across 1,000 cyclic loading cycles. In contrast, while the motorized virtual spring tracked commanded current smoothly, gear friction and backlash created an unmistakable deadband around zero displacement, causing noticeable stickiness and catches during teleoperation.

### 4.3 Kinematic Consistency and Smoothness
In simulation, operators reached toward four target poses. Performance was evaluated using joint standard deviation, DTW (trajectory distance, lower is more consistent), and SPARC (spectral arc length for smoothness, closer to zero is smoother). While Naive GELLO suffered high variance in null-space joints J2 and J4, the proposed method drastically suppressed dispersion. Consistency improved across all novice operators as well as the expert, and expert completion time significantly dropped from 6.56 s (Naive) down to 4.42 s.

### 4.4 Stiffness Sweep as Regularization Weight
Halving the spring thickness to halve stiffness ($K/2$) revealed that DTW error monotonically decreased ($24.20 \rightarrow 10.17 \rightarrow 6.86\text{ deg}$) as stiffness increased, confirming that mechanical stiffness acts directly as a regularization weight.

### 4.5 Downstream Imitation Learning (ACT) Performance
Policies were trained on a physical robot arm for Pick-and-Place and precision Block Stacking. Data from Naive GELLO showed more than double the joint DTW error, capping ACT success rates at 53.3% (Pick-and-Place) and 36.7% (Block Stacking). In contrast, the proposed method achieved 96.7% and 73.3%, respectively. In Block Stacking, where continuous fine adjustments are required, the absence of micro-catches from motor backlash gave the proposed passive arm significantly superior movement smoothness (SPARC).

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: Inexpensive 3D-printed springs provide physical regularization that substantially boosts teleoperation data quality and imitation learning success rates. Despite trade-offs like manual clutch adjustment and scaling to heavier arms, it offers a compelling new standard for robot data collection.
sections.details:
This work overcomes the joint posture inconsistency inherent to low-cost passive leader arms by turning the hardware itself into an optimization regularizer (Hardware-as-Regularization). By utilizing zero-latency, fully passive springs, it avoids the oscillation risks and backlash catches of active motors while delivering a dramatic boost in imitation learning success.

Several limitations and future challenges remain:
- Reconfiguring neutral postures: Unlike active motors reconfigured via software, adjusting the clutch screws manually across all 7 joints requires 2 to 3 minutes of downtime during task changeover.
- Operator fatigue across wide workspaces: While negligible in localized workspaces, tasks requiring large arm sweeps across the full reach may induce operator fatigue against the spring force.
- Scaling to larger robots: Counteracting larger follower arms requires thicker, stiffer springs, highlighting the need for compact packaging or metamaterial spring designs in future work.

Nevertheless, achieving such fundamental improvements in data consistency using only 3D-printed parts—without added motors or complex control loops—makes this an extraordinarily practical solution for real-world imitation learning pipelines.

sections.heading: Appendix: Detailed hardware specifications and spring mechanics
sections.summary: This section details joint kinematic configurations, spring design parameters for each axis, and beam-theory stiffness formulations. Higher-stiffness springs are deployed at joints subjected to greater gravitational loads.
sections.details:
### A.1 Arm Kinematics and Sizing
The leader and follower arms share an identical 7-DoF kinematic configuration, with the leader scaled to approximately 40% of the physical follower robot. Joint angles map directly at a 1:1 ratio.

### A.2 Spring Parameters per Joint
The baseline joint module uses a spring with width $b=8\text{ mm}$, thickness $t=1.5\text{ mm}$, and active turns $N=3$. For joints heavily loaded by gravity (J2 and J4), reinforced geometries are used:
- Joint 2: Width $b=30\text{ mm}$, thickness $t=2.5\text{ mm}$ (theoretical stiffness $0.344\text{ Nm/rad}$)
- Joint 4: Width $b=25\text{ mm}$, thickness $t=2.0\text{ mm}$ (theoretical stiffness $0.153\text{ Nm/rad}$)

### A.3 Spiral Spring Bending Formulation
The theoretical torsional stiffness $K$ of an Archimedean spiral spring fixed at both ends is derived from beam theory using the flexural modulus $E$, second moment of area $I = \frac{b t^3}{12}$, and unwound active length $L$:
$$
K = \frac{E I}{L} = \frac{E b t^3}{12 L}
$$
The active length $L$ of an Archimedean spiral is calculated geometrically from inner radius $r_{in}$, pitch $p$, and turns $N$. Because stiffness scales with the third power of thickness ($t^3$), a 3D printing tolerance variation of just $0.2\text{ mm}$ increases stiffness by a factor of roughly 1.45. This manufacturing tolerance and internal friction explain why measured stiffness values were slightly higher than nominal theory. Even so, intra-batch consistency was remarkably tight, confirming high fabrication reproducibility.

takeaways: The primary factor degrading demonstration quality in imitation learning teleoperation was null-space drift caused by unconstrained redundant joints.
Embedding mechanical springs into joints physically realizes mathematical $L_2$ regularization (Tikhonov regularization) by exploiting the human tendency to minimize muscular effort.
While inexpensive virtual springs built with servomotors suffer from micro-catches due to gear backlash, fully passive physical springs deliver zero-latency, exceptionally smooth teleoperation.
Increasing spring stiffness directly corresponds to increasing regularization weight, reducing demonstration variance and dramatically lifting downstream imitation learning (ACT) task success rates.
limitations: Changing the neutral posture ($q_0$) for different manipulation tasks requires manually loosening and retightening clutch screws (taking about 2 to 3 minutes across all 7 joints).
In dynamic tasks that span the full workspace, operators can experience muscular fatigue from constantly resisting spring forces during large reaches.

Downstream imitation learning was validated only using ACT; evaluating the impact on other architectures (such as Diffusion Policy) and benchmarking against active motors with PD control and backlash compensation remain future work.
